summary: FIREWATCH harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar for India from 2003 to 2026. VIIRS (375 m) detects about 7.8 times more hotspots than MODIS (1 km), so joining the two records naively creates a fake jump in 2012 and makes long-term trends misleading. We fitted 12 monthly MODIS-to-VIIRS ratios on the 2012–2018 overlap, scaled the earlier MODIS record onto the VIIRS S-NPP scale, and spliced in NOAA-20 after S-NPP ended. On held-out years 2019–2025, our method cut the error from 31,107 to 4,288 hotspots per month (MAPE 88.1% to 15.9%, correlation 0.98). Our web app lets anyone draw an area or enter coordinates and see which months and years burned most, compare this month with the historical median, explore trend, hot-spot cluster and chronic-burning map layers, read an AI summary of the numbers, see NASA POWER weather context, and download CSVs. This gives farmers, officials and researchers a fair long-term view of fire activity, such as the Punjab–Haryana stubble-burning season.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FIREWATCH turns two NASA satellite fire records into one comparable 23-year history for any area in India. Users draw a rectangle, circle or polygon on the map (or enter coordinates) and get: a burning-activity calendar (which months and years burned most, 2003–2026), trends, this month compared with the historical median (above the 90th percentile is flagged as unusual), spatial analysis layers (per-cell trend with Theil-Sen slope and Mann-Kendall test, Getis-Ord Gi* hot/cold-spot clusters, and chronic burning where fires recur in at least 80% of years), a hotspot map, CSV downloads, an AI-generated plain-language summary, and NASA POWER rainfall and temperature context.

Live app: https://firewatch-india.streamlit.app

Code: https://github.com/KRITHIKYADAV06/FIREWATCH

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: 11.5 million NASA FIRMS hotspots for India (MODIS C6.1 Aqua 2003–2025, VIIRS S-NPP 2012–2026, VIIRS NOAA-20 2018–2026), vegetation fires only (type 0), nominal/high confidence, gridded to 0.1°.

2. Harmonization: VIIRS detects about 7.8x more hotspots than MODIS, so joining the records naively creates a fake jump in 2012. We fitted 12 monthly VIIRS/MODIS ratios on 2012–2018, scaled earlier MODIS onto the VIIRS S-NPP scale, and spliced in NOAA-20 after S-NPP ended on 2 Nov 2026.

3. Validation on held-out 2019–2025 (India monthly totals): MAE 4,288 vs 31,107 for the naive splice and 8,758 for a single pooled ratio; MAPE 15.9% vs 88.1%; Pearson r 0.98.

4. Experimental ML forecast: gradient boosting predicts next month's fires per cell; on 2025 it scored MAE 1.28 vs 1.36 (same-month median) and 1.52 (same month last year), with a top-10% hit rate of 63%.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Without harmonization, "more fires" can simply mean "a better sensor". FIREWATCH gives farmers, district officials, researchers and journalists a fair long-term picture, for example of the October–November stubble-burning season in Punjab and Haryana, so that policies and trends can be judged on real change.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, SciPy, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Folium/Leaflet, Plotly, Google Gemini API, NASA POWER API, GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud, pytest (automated tests).

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

Season-specific ratios instead of one factor; an honest held-out validation against two baselines; zero detections treated as "no FIRMS detections", not "no fire"; the AI summary may only use our computed numbers and is labelled AI-generated; accessible colour palettes. Limitations: accurate for regional totals, not single 0.1° cells; data through 31 July 2026; near-real-time integration is future work.

TEAM

S Krithik Yadav (lead, data science & ML), Parth Pillai (data engineering), Avin ke (backend), Alisha Maharana (geospatial), Anthony Fernandes (frontend), Adrita Sarkar (testing & documentation).
